title: Handoffs & Delegation
summary: A handoff transfers control — and the relevant context — from one agent to another, so the second agent continues the conversation rather than just returning a value. The core decisions are when to hand off versus call another agent as a tool, and how to carry enough state across the boundary that the receiving agent isn't starting blind.

subtopics.title: A handoff transfers control, not just a result
subtopics.explanation: In a handoff, the current agent decides another agent should take over and passes the conversation to it; the new agent now drives the loop and talks to the user directly. This differs from a plain function call because control moves — the first agent steps back rather than waiting for a value. Understanding that control itself moves is the key to reasoning about who is responsible for the next turn.

subtopics.title: Handoff vs calling an agent as a tool
subtopics.explanation: Calling an agent as a tool is a request-response: you invoke it, get a value back, and keep control. A handoff gives up control entirely to the other agent. Use a tool call when you need a sub-answer to continue your own reasoning; use a handoff when a different specialist should own the rest of the interaction. Picking the wrong one either strands a conversation or forces one agent to babysit work it shouldn't own.

subtopics.title: Transfer the context, not the whole history
subtopics.explanation: The receiving agent needs enough of the prior conversation to continue, but dumping the entire transcript bloats its context and buries the point. A good handoff includes a compact summary of what happened, the user's goal, and any decisions already made. Choosing what context to carry is what determines whether the new agent picks up smoothly or has to re-ask the user everything.

subtopics.title: Preserve state across the boundary
subtopics.explanation: Facts established before the handoff — an authenticated user, a chosen product, a confirmed address — must survive so the new agent doesn't redo or contradict them. This means passing structured state (not just prose) that the receiving agent trusts and extends. Preserving state across the boundary is what makes a multi-agent conversation feel like one continuous experience rather than a cold transfer.

subtopics.title: Return handoffs and avoiding ping-pong
subtopics.explanation: Specialists often hand back to a coordinator when their part is done, so control can pass around several times in one session. Without guardrails this becomes ping-pong — agents bouncing a user back and forth — so you track a handoff count and route to a human or a default after a cap. Bounding the number of handoffs is what keeps delegation from degrading into an infinite transfer loop.

foundations.overview: A handoff is a transfer of control between agents: rather than returning a value to a caller, the active agent decides a different agent should take over the conversation, and the runner switches who drives the loop and talks to the user. This is distinct from calling an agent as a tool, where the caller stays in control and merely consumes a returned value. The two questions that define the pattern are when to hand off versus call-as-a-tool — hand off when a specialist should own the rest of the interaction, call-as-a-tool when you need a sub-answer to continue your own reasoning — and how to carry state across the boundary. A good handoff transfers a compact context (goal, summary, decisions) plus structured state (identity, selections, confirmations) so the receiving agent continues seamlessly instead of re-interrogating the user. Because control can pass repeatedly, robust systems bound the number of hops and provide return handoffs and a human fallback to prevent ping-pong.
foundations.formalDefinition: A handoff is an operation in which the currently active agent transfers control of a session to another agent, passing along the context and state needed to continue, after which the receiving agent drives the loop; it contrasts with agent-as-tool invocation, where the caller retains control and receives only a return value.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real assistants route between specialists — triage to billing to engineering — and doing that as handoffs (transfer of control) rather than nested tool calls keeps each agent focused and the conversation continuous. Getting the control model and state transfer right is the difference between a smooth escalation and a user forced to repeat themselves.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a phone support transfer. Calling an agent as a tool is putting the caller on hold, asking a colleague a quick question, and coming back yourself. A handoff is warm-transferring the caller to a specialist along with a note of who they are and what they need — the specialist now owns the call, and a good note means the caller never re-explains.
foundations.whenToUse: Hand off when a distinct specialist should own the remainder of the interaction (escalation, domain switch). Call an agent as a tool when you need its output to keep reasoning yourself. Prefer a single agent when the 'specialist' work is small enough to fold into the current one.
foundations.tradeoffs: Handoffs give clean separation of responsibility and focused specialists, but they add a transfer boundary where context can be lost, state can desync, and control can ping-pong; you mitigate with compact context transfer, shared structured state, and a hop cap with a human fallback.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Customer-support routing (triage -> billing/technical/returns), coding assistants that hand a failing build to a debugging agent, and sales flows that transfer a qualified lead from a chat agent to a scheduling agent — each carrying the prior context forward.
commonUseCases: Support triage escalating to a domain specialist
Handing a sub-answer back via agent-as-tool instead of transfer
Return handoff to a coordinator when a specialist finishes

commonMisconceptions.myth: A handoff is just a function call to another agent.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A function/tool call returns control to the caller; a handoff transfers control — the receiving agent now drives the loop and talks to the user.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should pass the entire transcript on every handoff.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Dumping raw history bloats context and buries the goal. Pass a compact summary plus structured state (goal, decisions, identity) instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Once you hand off, control can never come back.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Specialists commonly hand back to a coordinator; you bound total hops and add a human fallback to prevent endless ping-pong.

checkpoints.prompt: What fundamentally distinguishes a handoff from calling another agent as a tool?
options: A handoff transfers control so the receiving agent drives the loop, whereas a tool call returns a value and the caller keeps control
A handoff cannot pass any context
Tool calls can only be used once per session
checkpoints.explanation: Control is the distinction. In a handoff the active agent steps back and the new agent owns the next turns; in an agent-as-tool call the caller stays in charge and just consumes a returned value to continue its own reasoning.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this handoff make the user repeat themselves?
options: billing should not take a context argument
The handoff carries no context, so the goal and prior decisions are lost and billing has to re-interrogate the user
Handoffs are not allowed from triage
context must be a list, not a dict
checkpoints.explanation: Transferring control without transferring context strands the receiving agent. A good handoff carries a compact summary plus structured state (goal, decisions, identity) so billing continues seamlessly instead of asking the user to start over.

checkpoints.prompt: With max_hops=4 and two agents that always hand back to each other, what does run print?
checkpoints.code:
# triage -> billing -> triage -> billing ... each returns a Handoff
print(run("triage", State()))
checkpoints.explanation: Each hand-back increments state.hops; once hops exceeds max_hops (i.e. reaches 5) the runner stops the ping-pong and escalates to a human, and the verified flag set before the first handoff survives across every hop.

theory.question: When should one agent hand off to another versus call it as a tool?
theory.directAnswer: Hand off when a different specialist should own the rest of the interaction — control transfers and the new agent drives the loop and talks to the user (e.g. triage escalating to billing). Call an agent as a tool when you only need its output to continue your own reasoning — control stays with you and you get a return value (e.g. a planner asking a research agent for facts).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways one agent involves another: a handoff (transfer of control) and agent-as-tool invocation (request-response that returns control).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some work is a sub-question the caller should fold into its own answer; other work is a whole responsibility a specialist should own end-to-end. Modelling each correctly keeps agents focused and conversations continuous.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A handoff returns a transfer signal that the runner uses to switch the active agent, carrying context and state forward; an agent-as-tool call runs the other agent synchronously and returns its value while the caller stays active.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong either strands a conversation (tool call where a handoff was needed) or forces one agent to babysit work it shouldn't own (handoff where a tool call sufficed), both of which degrade reliability and UX.
theory.realWorldExample: A support triage agent hands off a refund request to billing (billing owns the conversation) but calls a knowledge-base agent as a tool to fetch a policy snippet it then uses in its own reply.

followUps.question: Can an agent-as-tool call itself trigger a handoff?
followUps.answer: The invoked agent returns a value, so any escalation it recommends is data the caller acts on; the caller decides whether to then hand off, keeping control explicit.

followUps.question: How do you decide granularity?
followUps.answer: If the 'specialist' work is small and tightly coupled to the current reasoning, fold it in or call as a tool; reserve handoffs for genuinely separate ownership.

theory.question: How do you preserve state across a handoff so the receiving agent doesn't start blind?
theory.directAnswer: Pass a compact context — the user's goal, a summary of what happened, and decisions already made — plus a structured state object holding facts like identity, selections, and confirmations, rather than dumping the raw transcript. The receiving agent trusts and extends that state so established facts survive and it continues the conversation seamlessly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The practice of carrying just-enough conversation context and a shared structured state across the control-transfer boundary.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Transferring control without transferring state forces the new agent to re-ask the user everything or, worse, contradict prior decisions, breaking the illusion of one continuous assistant.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Build a handoff payload with goal, a summary (not raw history), and prior decisions, and pass a typed state object (verified, cart, addresses) that the receiving agent reads and mutates rather than resetting.

theory.whyImportant: State preservation is what makes multi-agent conversations feel continuous; without it, escalations feel like cold transfers and users lose trust.
theory.realWorldExample: After a triage agent verifies a customer's identity, the handoff carries verified=True so billing issues the refund immediately instead of re-authenticating.

followUps.question: Why summarise instead of passing full history?
followUps.answer: Raw transcripts bloat the receiving agent's context, cost more tokens, and bury the actual goal; a compact summary keeps it focused and cheaper.

followUps.question: What risks come from shared mutable state?
followUps.answer: Concurrent or careless writes can desync agents; keep the state structured, document ownership, and validate invariants the receiving agent depends on.

scenario.question: Users complain that your support bot bounces them between agents and makes them repeat themselves. How do you fix the handoff design?
scenario.directAnswer: Attack two root causes. For repetition, make every handoff carry a compact context (goal, summary, decisions) and a shared structured state so the receiving agent continues instead of re-asking. For bouncing, track a hop count in the state and cap total handoffs, routing to a human or a sensible default when the cap is hit, and audit which agents hand back so the ping-pong pair can be merged or clarified.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reliability and UX problem where control transfers lose context and control cycles between agents.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Handoffs that transfer control but not state force re-interrogation, and specialists that hand back without progress create loops when routing rules overlap.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Add a handoff payload with goal/summary/decisions plus a typed session state, increment a hops counter on each transfer, and short-circuit to a human fallback past a cap; log handoff edges to find the cycle and fix the overlapping routing logic.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the two failure modes unique to delegation — lost context and control ping-pong — and the concrete guardrails (state transfer, hop cap, fallback) that production systems need.
scenario.realWorldExample: A bot looped triage->billing->triage because both claimed 'account' questions; adding a hop cap plus a shared state that recorded the resolved intent broke the loop and eliminated the repeated identity checks.

followUps.question: Where do you set the hop cap?
followUps.answer: Low enough to protect UX (often 3-4 transfers) with a human or default fallback, tuned by looking at real session logs of how many hops legitimate flows need.

followUps.question: How do you detect ping-pong automatically?
followUps.answer: Log each handoff edge and alert when a session revisits the same agent pair or exceeds a hop threshold, surfacing overlapping routing rules for repair.

keyTakeaways: A handoff transfers control: the receiving agent drives the loop and talks to the user, unlike a tool call that returns a value.
Hand off when a specialist should own the rest of the interaction; call an agent as a tool when you need a sub-answer to keep reasoning.
Carry a compact context (goal, summary, decisions) — not the raw transcript — so the new agent picks up smoothly.
Preserve structured state (identity, selections, confirmations) across the boundary so established facts survive the transfer.
Bound total handoffs with a hop cap and a human fallback to stop specialists from ping-ponging the user forever.
